title: Choose the visual world for Flock Together
question: The roll assigned House Meter. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: House Meter
options.lineage: Mid-century applause meters, broadcast VU desks, backlit gauge panels
options.thesis: The screen is one electromechanical instrument that measures the room, so a majority is a needle slamming over rather than a number in a list.
options.viewport: A full-bleed oxblood panel: silkscreened header with a lit ROOM OPEN lamp, the question set huge on one wide ivory meter face, a ballistic timer needle sweeping an engraved scale toward a red arc, and a grid of 20 tiny round player gauges that flick from rest to deflected as each answer lands.
options.risk: Instrument panels read cold and corporate if the needles do not move with real damped physics and the panel legends are set timidly.

options.label: Riso Overlap
options.lineage: Risograph spot-ink printing, two fluoro inks misregistered on toothy paper
options.thesis: Answers are flat spot-ink blocks, and where they overlap the inks multiply into a third colour, so a group is literally where the room's ink stacks up.
options.viewport: Cut-paper answer blocks in single spot inks scattered on paper ground, sliding into overlapping stacks at reveal so the densest ink pile is the winner.
options.case: Strong world and the ink-overlap metaphor is genuinely beautiful for clustering, but riso grammar has no native language for a countdown or a running tally, and its signature misregistration is a hover effect that a shared TV screen never triggers.
options.risk: Loses the timer and the tally, the two things the display must show every single round.

options.label: Sticker Album
options.lineage: Collector sticker-album spreads with numbered ghosted slots
options.thesis: Every player is a numbered slot printed with a ghosted outline, and answering fills it with a glossy sticker sitting proud of the page.
options.viewport: A numbered album spread where empty slots advertise exactly who has not answered yet, filling one glossy sticker at a time.
options.case: Solves the who-has-answered problem better than anything else on the table, and the nostalgia lands instantly with a party. But album slots are fixed positions by definition, so it has no grammar for rows re-sorting into ranked groups, which is the reveal.
options.risk: Fuses well for the lobby and poorly for the reveal, which is the actual product.

options.label: Night Instrument Six-Pack
options.lineage: Small-aircraft night instrument panel, six luminous gauges
options.thesis: Six calm luminous dials hold the room's trust through the round, read as a practiced cross-check sweep.
options.viewport: Two ranked rows of three luminous gauges on an ink-black panel, each owning one truth about the round.
options.case: Same material family as the assigned direction but a quieter, dimmer rendition of it. A cockpit's whole register is calm solitary trust through cloud, which is the exact opposite of fifteen people shouting at a screen, and it lands squarely in the near-black-plus-neon-accent cluster.
options.risk: Wrong emotional register for a party, and the darkest option in a screenshared video window.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: What a party game screen ships: rounded geometric sans, saturated purple-to-magenta gradient, bouncy card flips, confetti on the winner.
canonCard.viewport: Centred question card on a gradient field, answer tiles in a responsive grid, a circular countdown ring, confetti burst at reveal.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from every other phone-joins-the-TV game, but instantly legible to anyone who has played one.
